messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kwame is a 30-year-old curriculum designer who came to treatment months after the end of a violent relationship that, in his words, had “changed the shape” of how he moved through ordinary life. He had been living with a girlfriend whose drinking escalated over time, and the worst assaults happened in their apartment after she had been drinking heavily. He remembers one night with particular clarity: the sour smell of alcohol on her breath and clothes, a pan left burning on the stove until the apartment filled with a sharp burnt odor, and her taunting him about his family when he tried to leave the room. She mocked where he came from and made cutting comments about his family while hitting him. What stayed with him was not only the blows but the feeling of being trapped in a scene where the air itself seemed polluted by alcohol, smoke, and humiliation.

In the weeks after he left, seemingly small moments began to pull that night back into the present. A colleague making an offhand comment about family during a curriculum meeting, a student parent passing by with alcohol on his breath at an evening school event, or the faint burnt smell from an overheated office microwave could abruptly bring the event back with startling force. When that happened, Kwame did not just think about it. He felt pain in the same places in his body where he had been hit, as if his ribs and shoulders were remembering before his mind could get ahead of it. The terror was equally immediate. He would suddenly feel the same helpless fear he had felt in the apartment, and at times he could even smell alcohol or that scorched, burnt odor as vividly as if he were back there.

Those moments also carried a brutal meaning for him. A family-related remark was no longer just a remark; it seemed to confirm how deeply he had been degraded, that someone had used the most personal parts of his life to hurt him. The smell of alcohol or something burning could leave him thinking not only that he was unsafe, but that what happened to him had been profoundly unfair and that no one had answered for it. He found himself seized by a sense of contamination after these encounters, wanting to scrub his hands or stand apart from others, as though the relationship had left something unclean on him that had never washed off. He had come to believe that the man he was before the abuse was no longer available to him, that the version of himself now moving through the world—watchful, ashamed, easily shaken—was unrecognizable.

As the months went on, the memories themselves deepened these beliefs. Each time the scene returned with pain and terror, Kwame felt he was being shown evidence of what the abuse had done to him. If his body could still ache like that and his mind could still fill with the same smells, then to him it meant the experience had gotten inside him completely. He spoke with quiet anger about the injustice of it: she had assaulted him, yet he was the one still carrying the pain, still smelling the alcohol, still feeling dirty. The vividness of the recollections made it hard for him to dismiss any of this as being “in the past.” Instead, every resurgence of the memory seemed to prove that he had been altered in some essential way.

The memories also sharpened his sensitivity to the world around him. After enough episodes of catching that burnt smell in his mind when nothing was there, he became alert to any trace of smoke, singed food, or liquor in his environment. At work, where he spends long hours designing lesson sequences and meeting with teachers, he began scanning conference rooms and break areas before settling in. If someone joked about “what your family taught you” during a brainstorming session, he would stiffen immediately, already bracing for the bodily pain and terror that he had learned might follow. He started leaving meetings early if a custodian’s cleaning product carried an alcohol note, and he avoided staff happy hours altogether. These habits narrowed his work life and made him seem distant to coworkers, which only reinforced his sense that he was no longer himself.

By the time he sought help, Kwame was exhausted by how easily daily life could be pulled into the orbit of that relationship. He said what frightened him most was not only remembering the abuse, but the conviction that each reminder was showing him who he now was: damaged, contaminated, and left alone with something terribly unjust. He came in hoping, cautiously, that treatment might help him stop feeling ambushed by smells and comments that other people barely noticed, and that he might one day recognize himself again.
